html:
Cornelia was a Roman noblewoman who lived from about the 190s to about 115 BCE. She was the daughter of Scipio Africanus and the mother of the reformers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, and later Romans held her up as the ideal mother.

She married Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, a leading statesman, and had twelve children, but only three lived to grow up: the two brothers and a daughter, Sempronia, who married Scipio Aemilianus. After her husband died she refused to remarry, even turning down a king of Egypt, and gave herself to her children's education. A well known story tells how, when a visitor showed off her jewels, Cornelia pointed to her sons and said, "These are my jewels."

She was famous in her own right for her learning, and her letters were published and admired; Cicero praised her style. Both her sons were killed in the political violence over their reforms, and she lived on at a villa near Misenum. Rome set up a bronze statue of her, one of the first public statues of a real Roman woman; its base, inscribed "Cornelia, daughter of Africanus, mother of the Gracchi", survives.
